questions.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨0,\,0,\,-2y⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=4-x-2y.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and the plane $z=4-x-2y.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4-x-2y.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-x-2y)=-1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨0,\,0,\,-2y⟩{|}_{z=4-x-2y} \\  & =⟨{{0}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-2y}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-1)-0\cdot (-2)+(-2y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-palne is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ with radius $1$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}2r\cdot r\,\text{d}r \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot [{r}^{2}]_{r=0}^{r=1} \\  & =(1-1)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=x\,i-z\,k$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2},\,z=1.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i-z\,k \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\,i-1\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j+0\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(({t}^{2}-t)\,i-\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-2t)\,j) \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-2t)+(-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-t)(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{({t}^{2}-t)^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,x,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-x\cdot (-2y)+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\,2\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,k$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=x\,i+y\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-0\cdot \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {cos}^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=2z\,i+x\,j+3y\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2z\,i+x\,j+3y\,k \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t-12{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2{cos}^{2}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t-14{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-14{sin}^{2}⁡t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-14{sin}^{2}⁡t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-7(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-5+7\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-5t+\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =(1-5(2\pi )+0)-(1-5(0)+0) \\  & =-10\pi \end{aligned}
$$
